transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-09-24
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~42 mins
Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (CSM), Aneesa Khan (StratusHealth CTO), Liam O'Connor (Lead ML Eng), Maya Patel (SRE), Jordan Lee (Procurement)

Summary: Quick recap of benchmark runs comparing Redwood Dedicated + caching profiles vs baseline provider (BigCloudAI). Focus on latency p50/p95/p99, throughput (tokens/sec), and variability under burst loads.

Topics:
- Perf numbers: median and tail latency
- Throughput and batching strategies
- Cold starts / warm pools / KV caching
- Security and VPC questions (K M S, audit logs)
- Next runs and data sharing

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Jamie Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick check we all good on time?
[00:06] Aneesa Khan: yeah all good, thanks jamie.
[00:12] Carlos Mendes: cool, i'll kick off with the perf summary, we ran the three profiles you asked for, baseline is bigcloud full-precision, our runs were dedicated quant-8 with prefix cache and an extra batching window.
[00:27] Liam O'Connor: quick q, is that the same seq len as our prod sim? we used 4k variable.
[00:33] Carlos Mendes: good call, for the baseline run we matched 4k and also did a 2k run, the most representative is the 4k one.
[00:40] Maya Patel: reading the slides now, i see p50 of 120ms on redwood and 140 on baseline, is that median token or full response latency?
[00:49] Carlos Mendes: that's per-request end-to-end median for the typical 300-token prompts from your sample set, so full response. there is some noise on the baseline p95 though where they spike to ~720ms on our test.
[01:05] Aneesa Khan: the p99 numbers look close, baseline had 980ms and you had 1.1s, is that right?
[01:14] Carlos Mendes: yes, in one run our p99 was slightly higher, we think that was caused by cold-starts on one of our smaller nodes during the test window. we saw two cold-start events tied to scale-up events.
[01:27] Jamie Park: to be clear, when we force warm pools we see the p99 drop to about 830ms, so the warm pool / pre-warm policy helps.
[01:37] Liam O'Connor: can you explain why baseline sometimes has lower tail? their provider is doing shorter queues?
[01:43] Carlos Mendes: possible, their infra is more aggressively provisioning for each request which reduces tail but increases unit cost. our autoscale is slightly more conservative unless you enable burst capacity.
[01:56] Maya Patel: what about throughput numbers under sustained load? we care about tokens per second because of streaming use-case.
[02:02] Carlos Mendes: sustained throughput at 90th percentile: Redwood dedicated with batching got 3.2k tokens/sec across the pool, baseline was 2.1k tokens/sec on the same test rig. when we enabled async batching and increased batch size we hit 4.1k.
[02:20] Aneesa Khan: those are big differences, did you adjust batch size manually? we worry about latency impact for small requests.
[02:26] Carlos Mendes: yes we tested three batch configs, small (8), medium (32), large (128). small keeps median low but lowers throughput; medium is the sweet spot for your mix. we can set dynamic batching to prefer low-latency for <50-token requests.
[02:41] Jordan Lee: procurement question: does Dedicated include burst capacity or is that extra?
[02:47] Jamie Park: burst is optional add-on, but we recommended it for the first month to smooth cold-starts while we tune warm pools. i'll put exact pricing in follow-up.
[02:56] Liam O'Connor: curious about quantization — you used quant-8, did that affect quality? any regressions on rouge or semantic tests?
[03:03] Carlos Mendes: we ran our eval suite on your prompt/response set — quality delta was within tolerance for the 95% of cases, a handful of prompts had minor token shifts but no user-visible regressions in the eval prompts you shared. we'll send the detailed diffs.
[03:18] Aneesa Khan: can you share the raw response diffs? we'll want to run our own quickspot checks.
[03:23] Jamie Park: yes i'll attach the diffs and the raw logs in the spreadsheet.
[03:28] Priya Rao: small note, transcription of product names in the doc may be messed up, so the logs will be raw.
[03:33] Maya Patel: can you speak to K V cache behaviour? last time we saw cache misses on multi-turn flows.
[03:38] Carlos Mendes: sure — our KV cache persists per-connection and also supports prefix caching for identical system prompts. some of your multi-turn tests had different user tokens so cache hit rate dropped. we recommended canonicalizing system messages — that increases hit rate from 42% to 76% in our test.
[03:57] Liam O'Connor: is the K V cache encrypted at rest? we need K M S integration per compliance.
[04:02] Jamie Park: yes, in Dedicated we support customer key wrap via K M S and H S M integrations; the Private option gives you full control of keys and audit logs.
[04:12] Aneesa Khan: how about audit logs and SSO for devs?
[04:16] Priya Rao: we can provide SAML S S O and per-token audit trails, plus model-level RBAC. i'll drop the security pack doc after.
[04:25] Jordan Lee: on procurement timeline, if we move forward on Dedicated what's typical lead time?
[04:30] Jamie Park: for Dedicated it's about 4 weeks for initial capacity including peering, could be faster if you accept our standard terms. private on-prem is longer.
[04:39] Aneesa Khan: we ran a redwood vs baseline A/B in our pilot last week and saw that baseline had slightly more consistent p99 for single small requests; can you replicate that?
[04:48] Carlos Mendes: we dug into that — baseline kept more headroom per-instance which reduced queueing. if you want that pattern we can configure smaller batch windows and more reserved capacity, but that increases cost per token.
[04:59] Liam O'Connor: can you quantify cost difference for the small-batch low-tail strategy vs the throughput-optimized approach?
[05:05] Jamie Park: yes — rough ballpark from our runs: low-tail config is ~1.4x cost per token vs throughput-optimized when comparing identical traffic. we'll add exact numbers to the spreadsheet.
[05:15] Maya Patel: about cold starts — earlier you mentioned pre-warm pools, how many nodes do you recommend for our 500 qps baseline?
[05:22] Carlos Mendes: for 500 qps and your request size we recommend a baseline pool of 6 nodes with 2 reserved warm buffers to keep p99 under 1s. with burst enabled we add ephemeral nodes when load spikes.
[05:34] Aneesa Khan: one of our worries is V P C peering and egress cost. do you have guidance?
[05:40] Jamie Park: peering is standard, egress depends on your cloud region — we can co-locate regionally to minimize egress. also we support bringing your own V P C for Private deployments.
[05:48] Liam O'Connor: thanks, also please note some proper nouns were transcribed weirdly in the notes; i'll rely on the raw logs you share.
[05:55] Carlos Mendes: action items we captured are re-running with 16k context, longer seq-len, and a couple of stress runs with 2x and 4x burst to observe queuing dynamics.
[06:05] Jamie Park: perfect, let's recap next steps and owners: carlos runs extended tests, jamie sends pricing and diffs, aneesa shares traffic profile.
[06:15] Aneesa Khan: sounds good. last question — if we pin a model version for the POC can you guarantee reproducible perf across weeks? we saw some drift with baseline.
[06:25] Carlos Mendes: yes pinning model and kernel selection makes perf stable; the only drift would come from infra changes. we can lock kernel and quant profile for the POC.
[06:33] Priya Rao: we'll also enable detailed tracing for the next run so we can attribute latency to queue, compute, or network.
[06:40] Liam O'Connor: timeline for next check-in?
[06:42] Jamie Park: let's meet next Tuesday same time, 09-30, to review the extended runs.
[06:48] Aneesa Khan: works for us, thanks everyone.
[06:50] Jordan Lee: thanks.

End of transcript.

References mentioned: benchmark spreadsheet (link in follow-up), security pack doc (to be shared), pricing addendum for Dedicated + burst.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-recognitions (K V cache written with spaces, K M S spelled out), speaker labels are accurate most of the time but may show slight mis-attribution in a few places.
